blocks.content: SQL LIMIT covered capping how many rows come back. SQL DISTINCT covers a genuinely different problem, removing duplicate rows from a result entirely, rather than simply limiting the total count. These solve different problems and should not be reached for interchangeably.

This topic covers exactly what DISTINCT does across a full row versus a single column, a worked example, the real difference between DISTINCT and GROUP BY, and a genuinely important performance note, since DISTINCT is not actually free to compute on a large table.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200804-90255742.png
1. Without DISTINCT Versus With DISTINCT

A SELECT without DISTINCT returns every row that matches, including exact duplicates, if two rows genuinely have identical values across every selected column, both are returned, since SELECT alone makes no attempt to deduplicate anything.

A SELECT with DISTINCT returns only unique combinations of the selected columns, collapsing any exact duplicates down to a single row, which is genuinely useful when you care about which distinct values exist, not how many times each one happens to appear.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200805-117143123.png
2. A Worked Example

A concrete query shows DISTINCT applied to a real, common question. An orders table has a customer_id column, and a specific query needs to know which customers have ever placed an order, not how many orders each one placed.
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders;

This query returns each customer id exactly once, no matter how many separate orders that customer actually placed, genuinely answering the question of which distinct customers exist in the orders table, rather than listing every individual order row.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200806-289834887.png

{"headers":["Query","What It Actually Returns"],"rows":[["SELECT customer_id FROM orders","Every order row, customer ids repeated for each order"],["SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders","Each customer id exactly once, no repeats"]]}
3. DISTINCT Across Multiple Columns

DISTINCT genuinely considers the full combination of every selected column together, not just the first one listed. Two rows are only treated as duplicates if every single selected column matches exactly between them.

This matters a great deal in practice, SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, order_date does not just deduplicate by customer, it deduplicates by the specific combination of customer and date together, meaning the same customer can genuinely still appear multiple times, once for each distinct date they placed an order.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200807-903609000.png

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Forgetting that DISTINCT applies to the entire selected row, not just the first column listed. Adding more columns to a SELECT DISTINCT query genuinely changes what counts as a duplicate, often unintentionally increasing the number of rows returned.
4. DISTINCT Versus GROUP BY

DISTINCT simply removes duplicate rows, with no aggregation involved at all, it is genuinely the simpler of the two tools, appropriate when you just want to know which unique values or combinations exist.

GROUP BY groups rows together specifically to compute an aggregate value per group, a count, a sum, an average, something DISTINCT genuinely cannot do on its own. If you find yourself wanting a count alongside your unique values, that is a real signal you actually need GROUP BY, not DISTINCT, a distinction covered in real depth in the next module of this course.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200807-486196615.png
5. Why DISTINCT Is Not Genuinely Free
blocks.text: 5. Why DISTINCT Is Not Genuinely Free

blocks.content: A few real reasons DISTINCT carries a genuine performance cost worth understanding. The database must actually compare rows against each other to determine which ones are genuine duplicates, this comparison work is not free, even though it happens behind the scenes.

On a genuinely large table, this comparison work costs real, measurable time, sometimes requiring the database to sort or hash the entire result set internally just to identify the duplicates. DISTINCT is worth using deliberately, when you genuinely need deduplication, not as a reflexive habit added to every query just in case.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200808-163058483.png
blocks.alt: Why DISTINCT Is Not Genuinely Free

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A query that returns duplicates because of a genuine logic error, often a missing or incorrect join condition, should have that underlying error fixed directly. Adding DISTINCT on top of a broken query often just hides the real problem rather than solving it.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine DISTINCT usage. Using DISTINCT as a reflexive fix for a query that is actually producing duplicates because of a genuine underlying error, like a missing join condition, rather than fixing that real root cause directly. Forgetting DISTINCT applies to the full selected row, not just one column, leading to unexpected results once more columns are added to the SELECT clause.
And reaching for DISTINCT when GROUP BY is genuinely what the problem actually needs, specifically whenever an aggregate value like a count or sum is also required alongside the unique values.
